extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics faculty, curriculum designers, and academic administrators responsible for quantitative literacy programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for creating, implementing, placing students into, and assessing a college-level quantitative literacy requirement and associated courses. Covers program goals, learning outcomes/competencies, placement rules, course-level learning objectives, and assessment practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what it is you want to assess
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one of the assessment measures described above speaks directly to the problem that led to the implementation of QPS. The initial problem was students having difficulties in specific general-education courses requiring quantitative skills; many measures do not speak directly to performance in those specific subsequent courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a specific assessment measure before starting a program if possible. Institutional data (e.g., specific course grades for specific students) can be obtained but may require effort and may produce small samples; weigh the cost/benefit of collecting highly specific data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of variations in the population
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly at smaller institutions, any statistical study is affected by small populations. Aggregating cohorts with different beginning levels or ignoring retention can distort results; disaggregation reduces sample sizes further. Comparison groups may have un-identified traits that distinguish them from target students even when placement and standardized scores look comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cohort differences, retention effects, and small-sample limitations when designing assessment and interpreting results. Use caution when comparing groups and consider possible unobserved differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple assessment measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a variety of measures will increase the confidence you have in your conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect different types of data (placement scores, pre/post tests, course grades, retention, qualitative feedback). Examine collected information carefully — it may be valuable in unanticipated ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for ambiguous results
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment outcomes may be ambiguous; faculty may want to declare a program a failure or a complete success, but the data may not support definitive statements either way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for ambiguous or mixed outcomes and prepare stakeholders for nuanced interpretations rather than binary declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate understanding of quantitative analysis (program learning outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate understanding of quantitative analysis: understanding and analyzing quantitative information presented in various formats; involves reasoning by symbolic, numerical, or geometrical means; determining various ways to solve problems; and predicting possible consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design courses and assessments that require representation, reasoning, problem solving, and prediction across multiple formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent and interpret quantitative information (competency a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent and interpret quantitative information symbolically, graphically, numerically, verbally, and in written form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include activities and assessments requiring students to convert and interpret quantitative information across representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limitations of mathematical and statistical models (competency b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the limitations of mathematical and statistical models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and assess model assumptions, domain of applicability, and limitations in real-world contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand nature and history of mathematics (competency c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop an understanding of the nature and history of mathematics, its role in scientific inquiry and technological progress, and its importance in dealing with issues in the public realm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate historical/contextual examples and discussions of how mathematics interacts with other fields and public issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand rudiments of statistics (competency d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop an understanding of the rudiments of statistics, including sampling and hypothesis testing, and the uses of statistical reasoning in everyday life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure students learn sampling principles, hypothesis testing logic, and practical applications of statistical reasoning; use projects and real data when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement via department-designed Mathematics Placement Test
rubrics_metrics.description: All undergraduates entering were required to take a Mathematics Placement Test designed by the department; results determine course eligibility and the registration process blocks students from registering in courses for which the test indicates they are unqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use placement testing to align students with appropriate quantitative-literacy courses; design or adapt placement tests to local needs if standardized tests are unsatisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proficiency thresholds determine course eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The proficiency level required for enrollment in Fundamentals of Statistics or Finite Mathematics is lower than that required for Elements of Calculus I. The first two courses require material typically taught in a second-year high school algebra course; Elements of Calculus I requires a precalculus course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear, explicit proficiency thresholds for each course and allow prerequisite coursework for students who do not meet them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy: no college-level prerequisite for core courses except for proficiency/developmental needs
rubrics_metrics.description: No core curriculum course may have a college level prerequisite, except where a proficiency level must be demonstrated or a developmental course is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core curriculum design should minimize hidden prerequisites while still protecting course integrity when specific proficiencies are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge-based courses must integrate knowledge, foundational skills, and values
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the fifteen courses used to satisfy a knowledge requirement must also integrate knowledge with foundational skills and, if possible, values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing quantitative-literacy courses, explicitly link content to foundational skills (communications, critical thinking, quantitative analysis, information literacy, etc.) and to institutional values where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforce Foundational Skills (program-level requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Knowledge-based component has learning outcomes and competencies; each Knowledge-based course must reinforce the development of one or more Foundational Skills (communications, critical thinking, ethical awareness, information literacy, quantitative and qualitative analysis and research methods, technological literacy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map course activities and assessments to one or more foundational skills and document how the course reinforces them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core curriculum Values requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All students must complete at least one course addressing each of the core curriculum Values (Civic Engagement, Diversity, Justice, Spirituality/Faith).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure quantitative-literacy offerings can be integrated with or aligned to institutional values where appropriate, and track student completion of value-related requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-semester College Writing Seminar required (core structure implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-semester College Writing Seminar is required as part of the Knowledge component of the core.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate quantitative-literacy courses with writing and communication goals when possible, to support written modes of quantitative interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational and mathematical sciences requirement fulfillment (course groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: The computational and mathematical sciences requirement can be satisfied by successful completion of mathematics courses in Groups 3 through 6 or those more advanced; Groups 1 and 2 are remedial and not considered satisfying the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define course-grouping schemes that allow flexibility for student majors and preparation while ensuring minimum curriculum goals are met by designated groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial course sequencing (Groups 1 and 2 policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses in Groups 1 and 2 are considered remedial and are mandatory for students who place at those levels. Students placed in Group 1 must, upon successful completion of Basic Core Mathematics, enroll in Basic Algebra the following term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish clear remediation pathways and sequencing requirements for students who place into lower preparation groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course selection in consultation with academic advisor
rubrics_metrics.description: The final course selection is made in consultation with a student’s academic advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement advising procedures to help students choose the quantitatively appropriate course that fits majors/minors and career goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamentals of Statistics — course learning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning objectives include: (1) basic knowledge and understanding of standard statistical terms and tools and their limitations; (2) comfort with data sets and descriptive parameters; (3) understanding differences between random studies and observational studies and their outcomes; (4) ability to evaluate claims supported by statistics; (5) recognizing problems in surveys and sampling (sample choice, bias, non-response); (6) understanding association, correlation, and regression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course design may include group work, projects involving sampling student opinion, emphasis on representative samples, and a balance of 'whys' (interpretation) and 'hows' (computation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite Mathematics — course learning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning objectives include: (1) ability to analyze patterns in data and interactions among systems; (2) understanding basic models and applications (environment, growth, economics); (3) comfort with basic notions of graph theory and applications (planning, scheduling, optimization); (4) familiarity with coding and applications in communications and identity codes; (5) basic knowledge of voting theory and applications in social choice procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty may emphasize graph theory, linear programming, codes, or social choice depending on interests; group work and real-world projects are useful (e.g., studying municipal snow-removal plans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of Calculus I — course learning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning objectives include: (1) strong background in methods, techniques, and applications of differential calculus; (2) basic knowledge of antiderivatives and the Riemann Integral and their applications; (3) familiarity with non-trivial applications of calculus in life sciences, social sciences, and business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate in-depth applications each semester where feasible (minimization problems, population models, path optimization, cost modeling), while recognizing limited flexibility due to sequence demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program assessment should move from qualitative to formal measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The department previously used qualitative measures (faculty impressions, student evaluations, discussions with served departments) to evaluate effectiveness; the new university-wide core requires measuring effectiveness of each department and course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop formal assessment plans for core courses (aligned learning outcomes, measurable indicators, multiple measures), replacing primarily qualitative evaluation with systematic data collection and analysis.
